CEST-detectable metabolite candidates: pancreas

1 of 3 candidates clear the simulated with-vs-without contrast threshold (0.5%) at some field strength, by chemical exchange (downfield, +ppm) or by the relayed NOE (upfield, −ppm). 1 fall below it; 1 are unknown because no group had a verified reference rate, so nothing could be simulated. The threshold applies to our own simulation, never to a literature MTRasym.

  • Mobile protein/peptide amide pool (backbone amide): ✓ detectable (chemical exchange)
  • Hyaluronan (glycosaminoglycan): ✗ not detectable
  • L-glutamate: ? unknown (not simulated)

Excluded before simulation (not stored in the tissue): [model's own exclusion] Bicarbonate in pancreatic juice/secretions (80-140+ mmol/L, PMIDs 22046082, 20398666, 428831): a ductal/exocrine SECRETION flowing through the tissue, not stored in the parenchyma; excluded as a CEST target OF the pancreas tissue per the fluid/secretion rule.; [model's own exclusion] Glycogen (glycoCEST): NOT a documented stored pool in pancreatic parenchyma. No quantitative pancreatic-tissue glycogen assay surfaced; beta-cell glycogen is minor and glycogen CEST targets liver/muscle. Marked absent-with-reason rather than listed as a candidate.; [model's own exclusion] Glucose in pancreatic tissue: acinar/islet cells take up and metabolize glucose, but no direct parenchymal tissue glucose concentration >1 mM was found in the retrieved set; not listed rather than given an unsourced number.; [model's own exclusion] Glutamine, glycine, taurine, lactate, creatine in pancreatic tissue: searches returned no direct parenchymal concentration >1 mM in the retrieved abstracts; excluded rather than estimated without a number.; [model's own exclusion] ATP / phosphocreatine: 31P-resonance species, off-target for 1H CEST; no direct pancreatic 1H exchangeable-proton concentration found.; [model's own exclusion] PME/PDE (phosphomonoester/phosphodiester) and lipid CH2 MRS peak groupings: spectroscopic category labels lumping unrelated compounds, not definable molecules/polymers with a repeating unit.; [model's own exclusion] Insulin, glucagon, somatostatin: endogenous pancreatic peptides but present at ng/mg-protein (sub-mM) levels, below the 1 mM threshold.; [model's own exclusion] Gangliosides (PMID 10775425): lipid-anchored glycoconjugates with no clean repeating-unit exchangeable pool and no absolute >1 mM tissue value reported.

Mobile protein/peptide amide pool (backbone amide) — CEST: ✓ detectable (chemical exchange)

Concentration: 250.00 mM typical (~200-300 (amide-proton-equivalent)) animal evidence only

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: The APT amide pool is the mobile protein/peptide backbone, present in all soft tissue, so its presence in pancreatic parenchyma is well established even though no dedicated pancreatic APT imaging study surfaced. I report it as amide-proton-equivalent concentration (the CEST-relevant quantity), not as the molarity of whole protein molecules. Derivation: ~70% water in wet tissue (assumption); soft-tissue protein fraction ~15-20% dry weight (assumption) gives ~45-55 mg protein/mL aqueous tissue; dividing by mean backbone amide residue mass (~110 Da) yields ~400-500 total backbone amides/mL; taking ~50-60% as the mobile, CEST-accessible amide pool gives ~200-300 mM amide-proton-equivalent, n_exchangeable_protons=1 per equivalent unit. Estimate, not a measured pancreatic value.

Recommended field strength(s): 0.5 T, 1.5 T, 3 T, 5 T, 7 T

Robustness to input uncertainty: robust

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (backbone amide NH (peptide bond) [amide]: concentration 200-300 mM, kex 15-158 s−1) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.35-1.91%, 1.5 T: 1.06-5.36%, 3 T: 1.42-10.33%, 5 T: 2.06-14.44%, 7 T: 2.40-16.45%. Threshold 0.5%. Detectable even at the low corner.

Frequency-collision analysis:

  • Dominant problem: the 3.5 ppm APT amide is at 0.0 Hz separation from the HA N-acetyl amide at EVERY field (0.5-7T), flagged unresolvable in all overlap_warnings - the two are chemically indistinguishable, so any reported 'APT' is a composite of mobile protein + HA + MT.
  • At 0.5T the amide also blurs with the HA hydroxyl (~1 ppm, 53.2 Hz < 137.7 Hz linewidth). The -3.5 ppm rNOE pool sits upfield of water and is well separated from the downfield amide. Semisolid MT is flagged unresolvable (15946 Hz combined linewidth) at all fields.

Direct water saturation: Swept B1 0.5-0.75 µT gives a direct-saturation bandwidth of 21.3 Hz (0.5-1.5T) and 31.9 Hz (3-7T). The APT offset is 87.5 Hz at 0.5T (just outside the 21.3 Hz band) and 447-1015 Hz at 3-7T, far outside the band. Direct water saturation does not significantly mask the exchange contrast; MTRasym/AREX still advisable at 0.5T where the offset is smallest.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat:

  • Amide kex 65.5 s−1 is the median of 116 s−1 (human brain, PMID 40228056) and 15 s−1 (human in vivo, PMID 23008121) - both human in vivo, not phantom-borrowed, but neither is pancreas-specific and field/pH/temperature are unstated. The 15-158 s−1 spread is genuine in-vivo variability; the low-kex corner drops contrast to ~1.4% (3T) and ~2.4% (7T).
  • The rNOE effective rate 5 s−1 is from a phantom (PMID 25996515), a class-level effective NOE rate, not an in-vivo rate, and is borrowed for pancreas.

Optimized saturation sequence by field strength (derived from a Bloch-McConnell B1×Tsat sweep):

  • 0.5 T: B1=0.5 µT, Tsat=750 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — At 0.5T the amide offset is only 87.5 Hz from water; the slow-exchange pool (kex 15-158 s−1) peaks at low B1 and the sweep found 0.5 µT optimal. Longer Tsat does not help because the pool reaches pseudo-steady-state quickly at low B1. MTRasym is the natural extraction given low field and the 3.5 ppm amide-amide overlap.
    recommended sequence: 1.308% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 1.5 T: B1=0.5 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — At 1.5T the amide offset is 262.5 Hz from water, in the CEST-favorable slow-exchange window. The sweep still favors 0.5 µT - the slow-exchange peak is broad and the optimum sits at the low end of the grid. The longer 3 s Tsat is needed to reach steady state at low B1 and 1.5T. MTRasym or simple Lorentzian difference at +/-3.5 ppm is appropriate.
    recommended sequence: 3.828% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 3 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — At 3T the amide offset (447 Hz) is well into the slow/intermediate window where CEST contrast peaks. The sweep favors 0.75 µT, slightly above the lower fields, consistent with the B1 optimum shifting up with B0 as the Hz offset grows. The 3 s Tsat ensures steady state. MTRasym is the standard APT readout; AREX with a T1 map is preferred for cross-subject quantification.
    recommended sequence: 5.979% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 5 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — At 5T the amide offset is 700 Hz from water, firmly in the CEST-favorable slow-exchange regime. The B1 optimum stays at 0.75 µT (as at 3T); the exchange rate is unchanged so the B1 optimum shifts only modestly with field. The 3 s Tsat is retained. Multi-pool Lorentzian or AREX is advisable to address the amide-amide overlap.
    recommended sequence: 8.490% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 7 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — At 7T the amide offset is 1015 Hz, deep in the slow-exchange window where max contrast (9.73%) is reached. The B1 optimum remains 0.75 µT; the large offset makes direct water saturation negligible and the exchange-limited regime fully engaged. At 7T, multi-pool Lorentzian or AREX with a T1 map is preferred given the strong semisolid MT and 3.5 ppm amide-amide overlap. pTx with VOP presaturation improves B1 homogeneity.
    recommended sequence: 9.734% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note:

  • Swept B1 0.5-0.75 µT / Tsat 0.75-3 s place this in the slow-exchange, low-B1 regime where MTRasym at 3.5 ppm is the standard APT extraction. But the 3.5 ppm pool overlaps the HA amide exactly and the semisolid MT adds a large asymmetric background, so MTRasym alone is confounded. AREX (T1-normalized) is preferred for cross-subject quantification (liver APT literature).
  • Multi-pool Lorentzian/omega-plot fitting could in principle separate the pools, but the 0 Hz amide-amide separation makes full separation infeasible - the two are reported together as 'APT'.

Potential clinical impact

amide (APT, 3.5 ppm): 1 CEST/NOE application and 0 metabolite-change studies verified (0 human, 1 animal; 0 humans, 4 animals; 1 dropped by verification). APT/amide CEST has been applied only in preclinical 14 T mouse pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) models: one correlated amide CEST with tumor volume during slow growth (r=-0.63, p=0.003), one showed amide CEST rises after pulsed focused ultrasound. No human APT-CEST pancreas study and no independent amide-pool metabolite-change study in pancreatic disease were identified. Evidence is limited and preclinical.

Caveats / critique (12 points, 559 words) — 250 mM total mobile backbone amide for pancreas is a reasonable order-of-magnitude (intracellular protein ~200-400 mM), but I found no direct pancreatic-tissue …
  • 250 mM total mobile backbone amide for pancreas is a reasonable order-of-magnitude (intracellular protein ~200-400 mM), but I found no direct pancreatic-tissue measurement; it is an assumption. Contrast scales linearly with concentration, so a 2x error is a 2x error. The 200-300 mM uncertainty span is generous.
  • The rNOE/rNOE16 pools are also assigned 250 mM, but membrane-lipid CH2 should be the much smaller membrane concentration, not total protein; this would overstate rNOE16 if it were simulated. The rNOE16 group is NOT SIMULATED (no verified effective rNOE rate/offset), so no contrast can be claimed for it.
  • Classes are correct: backbone amide NH is a true amide (pKa 14-16, slow/intermediate); aliphatic C-H rNOE and membrane lipid CH2 rNOE16 are correctly non-exchangeable NOE pools. No major exchangeable proton neglected - terminal/side-chain carboxyls are deprotonated at pH 7.4 and carry no proton.
  • The membrane lipid CH2 (rNOE16) group was NOT SIMULATED because the table has no verified effective rNOE transfer rate for that specific upfield pool; its ~-1.6 ppm offset was not simulated. The 3.5 ppm shift is the median across brain/liver in-vivo measurements, not a pancreas-specific value.
  • In-vivo APT is reported at 3.5 ppm in brain and liver CEST (3T liver, 7T/9.4T brain, rodent brain). I found no pancreas-specific APT shift. Pancreatic pH/temperature are not well characterized, so 3.5 ppm is an extrapolation from other tissues. None.
  • Carboxyl groups (terminal COOH, Asp/Glu side-chains) are deprotonated at pH 7.4 and carry no exchangeable proton, as Agent 2 correctly stated. The two NOE groups are correctly non-exchangeable. verifying_citations: PMID 26391991 (claimed as 'Amide proton transfer (APTO) imaging of the human liver in vivo: a pilot study at 3.0 T') dropped

Concentration: 5.00 mM typical (~1-20 (disaccharide-unit-equivalent; estimated, presence documented, no absolute assay retrieved)) animal evidence only

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: No absolute hyaluronan content (umol/g or mg/g) was reported in the retrieved pancreatic abstracts, so I give an estimate and flag it as such. The 14T KPC study (PMID 35205746) shows pancreatic tissue/PDA microenvironment contains abundant hyaluronan measurable by GagCEST, correlating with histological HA (r=0.81); the decellularized-scaffold study (PMID 29742511) confirms GAGs are a preserved component of native rat pancreatic ECM. The CEST-relevant quantity is the disaccharide-unit-equivalent concentration (unit [4->3]GlcA-[3->4]betaGlcNAc), NOT the molarity of the intact HA molecule. For a fibrotic/PDA-bearing pancreas I estimate a disaccharide-unit-equivalent concentration in the low single-digit to low tens of mM; typical_concentration_mM=5 is a placeholder order-of-magnitude figure, not a measured value, with n_exchangeable_protons=2 per disaccharide unit (1 -OH on each sugar residue).

Robustness to input uncertainty: upper-bound only

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (N-acetyl amide NH (GlcNAc) [amide]: concentration 1-20 mM, kex 15-158 s−1; Glucuronic acid (GlcA) alcoholic O-H [hydroxyl]: concentration 1-20 mM, kex fixed at 600 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown)) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.00-0.12%, 1.5 T: 0.01-0.34%, 3 T: 0.03-0.54%, 5 T: 0.06-1.26%, 7 T: 0.10-1.90%. Threshold 0.5%. The point estimate is below threshold; only the high corner clears it.

Frequency-collision analysis:

  • The N-acetyl amide at 3.5 ppm is at 0.0 Hz separation from the mobile-protein amide at EVERY field - the two are completely indistinguishable in a CEST measurement (same collision as the APT verdict).
  • The HA hydroxyl at 1.0 ppm is 53.2 Hz from the APT peak at 0.5T (within the 137.7 Hz combined linewidth, blurs), but well separated at 3T+ (300 Hz vs 1050 Hz). The hydroxyl is a fast exchanger (600 s−1) with a small offset, so its line is broad and its contrast weak.
  • Semisolid MT is flagged unresolvable at all fields. Practically: the HA amide cannot be separated from the protein amide, and the HA hydroxyl is weak and broad.

Direct water saturation: Swept B1 0.5-1.5 µT gives direct-saturation bandwidths of 21.3 Hz (0.5-1.5T), 31.9 Hz (3-5T), 63.9 Hz (7T). The HA hydroxyl at 1.0 ppm is 50 Hz from water at 0.5T (just outside the 21.3 Hz band, near the direct-sat tail, partially masking the already-weak hydroxyl contrast), and 150/300/750 Hz at 1.5/3/7T (well outside the band). The amide at 3.5 ppm is far from water at all fields and unaffected by direct saturation.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat:

  • The hydroxyl kex 600 s−1 is borrowed from myo-inositol in human brain at 7T (PMID 20951217) - a different metabolite, tissue, and the abstract does not state whether it was phantom or in vivo. This is a class-level value, not HA-specific. The amide kex 65.5 s−1 is borrowed from generic amide in vivo (brain, human). Neither is HA-specific or pancreas-specific.
  • Sugar-hydroxyl exchange is especially sensitive to pH/temperature, and ECM HA sits in a different ionic environment than free brain myo-inositol, so 600 s−1 may not reflect the true in-vivo HA hydroxyl rate in pancreas. The rNOE group was not simulated, so no rNOE rate caveat applies.

Optimized saturation sequence by field strength (derived from a Bloch-McConnell B1×Tsat sweep):

  • 0.5 T: B1=0.5 µT, Tsat=750 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.026% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 1.5 T: B1=0.5 µT, Tsat=2000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note:

  • No field strength reaches the 0.5% threshold for the whole metabolite (best 0.486% at 7T), so no sequence recommendation is issued. In the literature, GagCEST is extracted with MTRasym (PMID 35205746, 14T PDA). The hydroxyl at ~1 ppm can be targeted with a dedicated low-offset saturation at higher B1 (ViscoCEST, PMID 27071650: 3.6 µT, 1 s).
  • The amide at 3.5 ppm would use MTRasym but is confounded by the protein-amide overlap; multi-pool Lorentzian fitting is needed but the 0 Hz overlap makes full separation infeasible.
  • The swept B1 (0.5-1.5 µT, 750-3000 ms) is in the low-B1 slow-exchange regime suited to the amide; the faster hydroxyl (600 s−1) would benefit from higher B1, which the sweep did not explore for this metabolite.

Caveats / critique (12 points, 507 words) — 5 mM hyaluronan is a plausible ECM fraction for normal pancreas, though PDA desmoplastic stroma elevates HA (PMID 35205746 shows HA up in advanced PDA, correlat…
  • 5 mM hyaluronan is a plausible ECM fraction for normal pancreas, though PDA desmoplastic stroma elevates HA (PMID 35205746 shows HA up in advanced PDA, correlated with fibrosis). The 1-20 mM uncertainty span is generous.
  • Concentration is the limiting factor: 5 mM gives contrast ~50x smaller than the 250 mM protein amide pool, keeping all groups below the 0.5% threshold (best 0.486% at 7T, from the GlcA hydroxyl).
  • The rNOE group was assigned 5 mM with 13 protons, but for a macromolecule the concentration should be per-repeating-unit; the simulation flagged n_protons=13 as implausible and did not simulate it. Chemistry is well-reasoned. The N-acetyl amide NH (GlcNAc) is correctly classed amide, slow/intermediate, 3.5 ppm - the principal HA CEST handle.
  • The five hydroxyl O-H (3 GlcA + 2 GlcNAc) are correctly classed hydroxyl, fast, ~1 ppm. GlcA carboxyl correctly non-exchangeable (deprotonated). The glycosyl C-H rNOE pool is correctly non-exchangeable. One issue: the rNOE group (n_protons=13) was flagged implausible (not a per-repeating-unit count) and was NOT SIMULATED. No exchangeable protons neglected.
  • The ppm estimates (0.9-1.0 ppm hydroxyl, 3.5 ppm amide) are consistent with the literature (PMID 27071650 shows the HA hydroxyl CEST peak at ~0.8 ppm). The HA hydroxyl CEST peak is at ~0.8 ppm in phantom viscosupplement studies (PMID 27071650, 7T), consistent with Agent 2's 0.9-1.0 ppm.
  • The HA N-acetyl amide at 3.5 ppm is borrowed from the generic amide class; I found no independent HA-specific amide shift measurement. The 14T PDA study (PMID 35205746) reports 'GagCEST' without stating the exact ppm offset in the abstract, so the in-vivo HA amide/hydroxyl shift in pancreas is not directly confirmed from its abstract. None.
  • HA's only exchangeable groups are the sugar hydroxyls (5 O-H) and the N-acetyl amide NH, all identified. The GlcA carboxyl is deprotonated (no proton) and the glycosyl C-H are non-exchangeable - correctly excluded.
  • Groups not simulated: GlcA carboxyl (COO-) [other] -- the chemist judged this group not exchangeable with water; not simulated; glycosyl C-H + N-acetyl CH3 (glycoNOE/rNOE) [rnoe] -- not simulated: Hyaluronan (glycosaminoglycan): n_exchangeable_protons=13 is not a per-molecule (or per-repeating-unit) proton count.
  • Use 1-12; for a polymer or macromolecular pool give the concentration PER repeating unit (e.g. glycogen ~250-300 mM glucosyl units x 3 hydroxyl protons; the mobile-protein amide pool ~200-300 mM x 1), not a whole-molecule count. no SAR or hardware ceiling is applied: the recommended B1/Tsat is the sweep optimum, and deliverability must be checked against the scanner's SAR monitor
  • gagCEST target. Pancreas is a non-cartilage tissue, so GAG load is low-to-moderate and rises sharply in fibrosis/PDA. Value is a disaccharide-unit-equivalent estimate, not the molarity of whole HA molecules; quantitatively uncertain pending a direct assay.
  • [Eligibility] typical_concentration_mM (5 mM) looks like the intact macromolecule's own molarity rather than its exchangeable-proton pool concentration -- this survived the re-emission check meant to catch it, so the simulated contrast for this metabolite is likely a severe underestimate.
  • [Unsourced reasoning] 2 numeric step(s) rest on an unsourced assumption: 'Report the disaccharide-unit-equivalent (unit [4->3]GlcA-[3->4]betaGlc'; 'No absolute HA assay retrieved; assign a low-single-digit-to-low-tens-'.

Robustness to input uncertainty: unknown

Uncertainty corners: Nothing was simulated for this metabolite (no exchangeable or rNOE group with a verified reference rate), so detectability is unknown -- not 'no'.

Frequency-collision analysis:

  • The amine group was NOT SIMULATED, so no field-specific overlap diagnostics were generated. Qualitatively, if the glutamate amine sits at 3.0 ppm in vivo, it is 0.5 ppm (375 Hz at 3T, 750 Hz at 7T) from the APT peak at 3.5 ppm - resolvable at 3T+ but close at 0.5T (~12.5 Hz).
  • At 0.5T a 2 ppm offset (~100 Hz from water) would also sit near the HA hydroxyl (~1 ppm). The fast-exchange amine (kex >> 2*pi*offset) produces a very broad, weak line, worsening overlap with APT and MT.

Direct water saturation: No direct-saturation bandwidth was computed because the amine was not simulated. Qualitatively, a fast-exchanging amine at ~2-3 ppm is close to the water direct-saturation tail, especially at low field: at 0.5T a 2 ppm offset is ~100 Hz, within the tail of a ~20 Hz core, masking the weak exchange contrast; at 3T the 2 ppm offset (~134 Hz) is well outside the ~32 Hz bandwidth, so masking is less severe.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: No exchange rate was simulated because the reference table has no verified kex or shift for the glutamate amine. The exchange rate is unknown and no contrast can be claimed. The literature GluCEST studies (PMID 32926951, 35299614) use MTRasym at 3.0 ppm and implicitly assume a fast-exchange amine but do not report a kex for glutamate. I did not supply a value from memory.

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note:

  • No B1/Tsat was swept because the amine group was not simulated. In the literature, GluCEST is extracted with MTRasym at 3.0 ppm followed by Lorentzian difference (to remove asymmetric MT) and AREX (to remove T1 bias), as in PMID 35299614.
  • This multi-step extraction is required because the glutamate amine is a fast exchanger with a small offset: its peak is broad, weak, and overlaps APT and semisolid MT. Without a verified kex and shift, no extraction method can be recommended for pancreas.

Caveats / critique (9 points, 436 words) — 2500 mM glutamate in pancreas is high. Pancreas is the major glutamine synthetase site, so the bulk nitrogen is glutamine, not glutamate; cytosolic glutamate is…
  • 2500 mM glutamate in pancreas is high. Pancreas is the major glutamine synthetase site, so the bulk nitrogen is glutamine, not glutamate; cytosolic glutamate is more typically a few hundred mM to low millimolar. If the true concentration is 100-500 mM, contrast scales down proportionally. However, even at 2500 mM, the missing reference kex/shift is the limiting factor, not concentration.
  • No pancreas-specific glutamate CEST or MRS-CEST study was found. Agent 2 correctly identifies the alpha-amino NH3+ (pKa 9.7, protonated at pH 7.4, three protons, fast exchange) as the only exchangeable group and correctly marks both carboxyls as deprotonated (no proton).
  • The amine group was NOT SIMULATED because the reference table has no verified exchange rate and shift for amine protons - an honest gap, not a chemistry error. The 2.0 ppm solution-NMR estimate is at odds with the in-vivo 3.0 ppm reported in GluCEST (see in_vivo_frequency_note); no verified value was simulated, so this discrepancy did not enter the numbers.
  • No exchangeable protons neglected. GluCEST signal is observed at 3.0 ppm in the literature (PMID 32926951 rat 7T; PMID 35299614 human 7T), not at the 2.0 ppm solution estimate from Agent 2. The in-vivo amine is shifted downfield relative to solution, likely from ionic/protein/crowding effects.
  • At 3.0 ppm it is 0.5 ppm from the 3.5 ppm APT peak (resolvable at 3T+ but close at low field). No verified reference value existed, so no shift was simulated. None. Both carboxyls are deprotonated at pH 7.4 and carry no proton (correctly excluded).
  • The only exchangeable group (alpha-amino NH3+) was identified but could not be simulated for lack of a reference kex/shift.

In vivo verification: ROI-differential CEST scan — axial slab, 24-32 mm thick, centered at the pancreatic body / portal-vein confluence level, parallel to the diaphragm

Why this scan:

  • A single axial mid-abdomen slab at the portal-vein/pancreatic-body level contains the target pancreas plus liver, spleen, one kidney's cortex, and paraspinal muscle. Total mobile protein/peptide (backbone amide) concentration is known to differ substantially across these tissues (muscle lowest, renal cortex highest).
  • If the 3.5 ppm APT dip and the -3.5/-1.6 ppm rNOE mirrors track that protein ranking while the 0/8 ppm baselines stay flat, the offset-specific contrast is the protein amide pool rather than a generic, tissue-uniform MT/NOE background (which would look similar across ROIs at a given offset).
ROIWhere it is drawnRole

Scan protocol: 3 T, pulsed rectangular train (duty-cycled, not CW), B1=0.9 µT, 40 pulses × 75 ms (interpulse delay 150 ms, duty cycle 33.3%), total Tsat=9000 ms, TR=9350 ms

SAR reasoning (the experimentalist agent's own; the pipeline applies no SAR model): At 3 T whole-abdomen SAR scales with B1^2 * duty; a mean on-pulse B1 of 0.90 µT at only 33% duty keeps average absorbed power below ICNIRP-2010 whole-body (2 W/kg) limits, and the 9.4 s TR spreads absorption in time between readouts. The abdominal coil is loosely loaded, keeping SAR below chest/limb extremes. Feasible for a single-slab multi-offset acquisition.

Compromise rationale:

  • The backbone amide CEST dip at 3 T is in the slow-to-intermediate window (kex ~1-20 s−1), whose optimum is NOT to over-rotate into the no-exchange limit (physicist: 0.75 µT / 3000 ms).
  • My single compromise of 0.90 µT over ~9 s total saturation sits just above that, keeping the amide pool in the CEST-active window (~6% with-vs-without) while the long on-time and duty cycle push the non-exchangeable rNOE pools (-3.5 mobile C-H, -1.6 membrane CH2) to their steady state, which favors the rNOE mirrors.
  • Slightly oversaturates the amide (marginally shallower APT) and undersaturates nothing, since only the protein pool is targeted.

Fat suppression: SPIR/SPAIR spoil-IR prepulse plus water-selective CEST excitation. The mid-abdomen has peripancreatic, perirenal, mesenteric and subcutaneous fat; the 1.3-1.6 ppm fat peak would fold into the 3.5 ppm APT asymmetry and corrupt the -1.6 ppm membrane-rNOE mirror, so a fat-suppressed water-only readout is required.

Motion mitigation: Timed-breathing navigator-gated (acceptance band ~+/-5 mm) acquisition on the diaphragm, since the pancreas and upper abdomen ride the respiratory diaphragm. Gating rejects ~20-40% of TRs, inflating the ~95 s/offset-set Z-spectrum (10 offsets) toward ~25-30 min total; single breath-hold is infeasible at this TR. Aortic pulsation near the uncinate/splenic vessels is a secondary, uncorrected confound.

Slice coverage: One axial slab, 24-32 mm thick (single 24 mm slice or 2×16 mm, no gap, to keep at least one kidney's cortex in-plane), centered at the pancreatic body / portal-vein confluence level, parallel to the diaphragm. FOV 380×380 mm, in-plane ~2×2 mm, thick enough to include the pancreatic body, mid right/left liver lobes, the medial splenic edge, one renal cortex, and posterior erector spinae muscle in the same field of view.

Structures in FOV: Pancreas, Liver, Spleen, Kidney (cortex/medulla), Paraspinal muscle, Aorta, Inferior vena cava, Subcutaneous and perirenal fat, Vertebral body

Differential analysis plan:

  • Extract ROI-averaged Z-spectra, apply WASSR B0/B1 correction, and compute MTRasym(delta) = [S(-delta)-S(+delta)]/S0 at 3.5, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0 ppm, plus raw MTR at 0 and +/-8 ppm and a Lorentzian-difference APT curve to separate amide from the rNOE shoulder.
  • Build a ROI x offset contrast matrix and test: (1) CONFIRMED if the 3.5 ppm MTRasym and the -3.5/-1.6 ppm rNOE mirrors rank paraspinal muscle < pancreas < liver < spleen < renal cortex, tracking the derived protein concentrations (correlation r>0.7), while the +/-8 ppm baseline stays flat across ROIs
  • (2) INCONCLUSIVE if the 3.5 ppm contrast is flat across ROIs, or the +/-8 ppm baseline varies strongly (dominant B1/T2/MT confounding), or the rNOE mirror does not invert with fat content. A paired 3.5-vs-2.0 ppm with-mirror comparison within each ROI localizes the dip to the amide.

Not actively targeted: Hyaluronan (GAG) and L-glutamate were explicitly flagged as low/no simulated contrast at all fields and were not actively designed around. At the single 0.90 µT / 9 s compromise, GAG (0.5-2 ppm, very slow exchange) and glutamate (~2.1 ppm, only 1-2 mM, tiny pool) would be far too weak to reach APT-level contrast here; a dedicated long-Tsat/low-B1 GAG scheme would double scan time and push SAR over the abdominal budget. Revisit in a separate dedicated acquisition.

Caveats:

  • Partial volume: pancreas (~3 cm) and the renal cortical rim (~1 cm) average duct, peripancreatic fat and medulla at 2×2 mm in-plane, blurring the protein ranking - the main quantitative risk. B0/B1 inhomogeneity across the 380 mm FOV persists even after WASSR; the pipeline's 0.7x/1.3x B1 re-simulation bounds how much predicted contrast survives.
  • Bone (vertebra/rib) and bowel gas near the pancreatic head cause local B0 shifts and dropout; the navigator corrects respiration only, not pulsation/gas. The 0.90 µT / 9 s compromise favors the rNOE mirrors and slightly oversaturates the amide, so APT depth is marginally below the physicist's 0.75 µT optimum.
  • All organ concentrations are derived (cellularity/water-based), not measured; the ROI ranking (the actual test) is robust even if absolute values shift.
